n: Job continues: I’ve seen and heard everything you’ve described about God’s power. I understand it.

f.w: mine eye hath seen all this
f.g: Referring to his description of God’s power in chapter 12.

n: Whatever you know, I know too. I’m not beneath you.

f.w: I am not inferior unto you

n: But Job doesn’t want to argue with his friends — he wants to speak directly to God and make his case. This is a bold act of faith: he still believes God will listen.

f.w: I desire to reason with God

n: You smear me with lies; you’re all worthless doctors. Their “medicine” only makes him worse.

f.g: Those who plaster over truth with falsehood.

n: If only you would be completely silent — that would be the wisest thing you could do! Their seven days of silence (Job 2:13) was their best counsel.
Now listen to my argument and pay attention to my case.
Will you lie to defend God? Job makes a deep point: God doesn’t need to be defended with falsehoods.

f.w: Will ye speak wickedly for God?
f.g: Defending God with untruths dishonors Him.

n: Will you show favoritism to God, acting as His lawyers? God does not need biased advocates.
Would it go well if God examined you? Can you fool Him as you might fool a man?
God will surely rebuke you if you secretly show partiality. This comes true at the end of the book, when God rebukes the friends (Job 42:7).
Shouldn’t God’s majesty terrify you and fill you with dread?
Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are as weak as clay.

f.g: Defenses (like shields or walls) made of clay — easily broken.

n: Be quiet so I can speak — come what may. Job is ready to accept whatever happens.

f.w: let come on me what will

n: Why should I risk my life? Two idioms for taking a great risk. Job knows challenging God is dangerous, but he is willing.

f.w: take my flesh in my teeth
f.g: An idiom for risking everything, like an animal carrying its prey.

f.w: put my life in mine hand

n: One of the great statements of faith in scripture: “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” Even facing death, Job holds on to God — while still insisting on his own integrity.

f.w: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him

f.g: Defend my conduct, argue my case.

n: Job believes God will be his salvation, because a godless person would never dare to come before Him. Approaching God at all is evidence of his sincerity.

f.w: He also shall be my salvation

n: Listen carefully to what I am about to say.
I have prepared my case, and I know I will be found innocent. Job is confident in his integrity.

f.g: I will be declared in the right.

n: Who can bring charges against me? If someone could, I would fall silent and die.
Turning to God, Job asks for just two things, so he can come before Him without hiding.

f.w: do not two things unto me
f.g: Grant me two requests (listed in verse 21).

n: First: take your hand of suffering off me. Second: stop terrifying me. Then he could face God.

f.w: Withdraw thine hand far from me

n: Then call me, and I’ll answer — or let me speak, and you answer me. Job asks for a real conversation with God.

f.w: Then call thou, and I will answer

n: How many sins have I committed? Show me my wrongdoing. Job honestly invites God to reveal anything he has done wrong.

f.w: make me to know my transgression

n: Why do you hide your face and treat me like an enemy? God’s silence hurts Job more than his sores. In Hebrew, “enemy” (oyev) sounds much like “Job” (Iyyov).

f.g: Hebrew oyev — a wordplay on Job’s name, Iyyov.

n: Will you frighten a leaf blown by the wind? Will you chase dry straw? Job feels weak and insignificant.
You write bitter charges against me and make me pay for the sins of my youth. Job wonders if old mistakes are being held against him.
You put my feet in shackles and watch every step, even marking the soles of my feet. He feels like a closely guarded prisoner.

f.g: Wooden restraints for a prisoner’s feet.

f.w: settest a print upon the heels of my feet
f.g: Mark or trace my footprints — tracking every move.

n: Meanwhile, man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment. This verse leads into chapter 14’s reflection on human frailty.

f.w: as a garment that is moth eaten
